system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2130-10-20 22:44:00 to 2130-10-22 14:51:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, PTSD, bipolar disorder, and prior abdominal surgeries was admitted for a recurrent incarcerated incisional hernia causing severe pain, nausea, and vomiting. He underwent successful open repair with mesh placement. Postoperatively, he developed mild atelectasis and leukocytosis, both managed conservatively. The incision showed blanching erythema, prompting a course of oral cephalexin, but no signs of active infection. He progressed well on pain control, diet advancement, and ambulation. By discharge, he was afebrile, tolerating a regular diabetic diet, ambulating independently, and had adequate pain control on oral medications. He was discharged home with instructions on wound care, activity restrictions, and follow-up with his surgeon and PCP.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Postoperative vomiting, please evaluate for small-bowel
obstruction.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to radiograph performed ___.

FINDINGS:  Supine and upright frontal radiographs is limited due to body
habitus.  However, there is no appearance of dilated small bowel, air-fluid
levels or pneumoperitoneum.  Air is noted within the large bowel to the level
of the rectum.  Surgical clips are in the right upper quadrant.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of bowel obstruction.

INDICATION:  Nausea, vomiting after status post nasogastric tube placement,
please evaluate position.

FINDINGS: Nasogastric tube is in stomach with side port beyond the GE
junction. Gas is noted throughout the small and large bowel without evidence
of dilatation.  Surgical clips are noted in the right upper quadrant.  No
pneumoperitoneum evident.

IMPRESSION:  Nasogastric tube in stomach with side port beyond GE junction. 
Non-obstructive bowel gas pattern.

INDICATION:  Vomiting, postoperative.  Also has abdominal distension. 
Evaluate for small bowel obstruction versus abscess versus rupture.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images were acquired from the lung bases through the
ischial tuberosities following the administration of both oral and intravenous
contrast material.  Multiplanar reformations were performed.

COMPARISON:  Reference CT abdomen from ___.  CT abdomen/pelvis from
___.

FINDINGS:  Aside from minimal bibasilar dependent atelectasis, the visualized
portions of the lungs are clear.  

The liver is grossly unremarkable.  There is no intrahepatic biliary duct
dilatation.  The portal vein is patent.  The patient is status post
cholecystectomy.  The spleen is normal in appearance.  The adrenal glands are
unremarkable bilaterally.  The kidneys are unremarkable aside from small right
renal hypodensities that are too small to characterize. Multiple punctate
calcifications are seen throughout the pancreas, consistent with known
diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis.  The pancreaticojejunostomy is
unremarkable.  There is no peripancreatic fat stranding to suggest acute
pancreatitis.  

An NG tube is seen extending into the stomach, ending near the antrum.  The
stomach is otherwise unremarkable.  The patient is status post a roux-en-Y
procedure.  Mild dilatation of a loop of small bowel adjacent to the
jejunojejunal anastomosis was seen on prior CT from ___, and likely
reflects postoperative change.  The small bowel and colon are otherwise normal
in appearance.  There is no free fluid or free air in the abdomen.  No
pathologically enlarged abdominal lymph nodes are seen.  The aorta is normal
in caliber and its main abdominal branches are widely patent.

Along the anterior abdominal wall in the region of the ventral incision, are
three rim-enhancing fluid collections that appear discrete, although subtle
communication cannot be excluded.  The largest collection, measuring 6.6 x 2.8
x 5.0 cm, is deep to the hernia repair mesh and has a focal protrusion into
the anterior abdominal wall subcutaneous fat (2:42).  This collection contains
two foci of air (2:32,34).  The second collection within the subcutaneous fat
to the right of the mesh measures 1.3 x 7.7 cm (2:44).  The third collection
measures 4.0 x 1.8 cm and is intraperitoneal and to the left of the mesh
(2:36).  There is extensive fat stranding within the anterior abdominal wall
adjacent to these collections.

PELVIS CT:  The bladder and prostate are unremarkable.  There is no free fluid
in the pelvis.  No pathologically enlarged pelvic lymph nodes are seen.

BONE WINDOW:  No suspicious lytic or blastic lesions are identified.  A
hemangioma is seen within the L2 vertebral body.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Three likely discrete rim-enhancing fluid collections within the anterior
abdominal wall, in close vicinity to the ventral incision/mesh, are concerning
for abscesses.   

2.  No additional acute intra-abdominal or pelvic pathology, otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I got kicked in the stomach by my brother a few days ago. Since then, I’ve had bad pain in the middle of my belly, and I’ve been throwing up—black and yellow stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this for about four days? And you haven’t been able to keep anything down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I tried sipping water, but it just comes back up. The pain’s getting worse, especially around my incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned an incision—was that from your hernia surgery three weeks ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had mesh put in. It was healing okay until this happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to keep you from eating or drinking for now to let your stomach rest. We’ve placed a small tube through your nose into your stomach to help with the vomiting. It’s called an NG tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt that. It’s uncomfortable, but I guess it helps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It does help by removing the pressure and fluid buildup. We also did an X-ray to check the tube’s position and to see if there’s a blockage. It’s in the right place, and there’s no sign of a bowel obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my intestines being blocked again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the X-ray shows gas moving through, so that’s good. But we’re concerned about infection near your surgical site. We ordered a CT scan with contrast to get a better look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? But I don’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s true, and your white blood cell count is normal, which is reassuring. But sometimes infections can develop even without fever, especially after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What happens if it is infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat it with IV antibiotics and monitor you closely. The CT will help us decide if there’s fluid that needs to be drained.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT results are back. There are three fluid collections near your incision and mesh. They have a rim-enhancing pattern, which raises concern for abscesses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Abscesses? Like pus pockets?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But the good news is you’re stable—no fever, normal labs, and your belly isn’t rigid. We’re going to treat this with IV antibiotics and keep you NPO for now. Surgery isn’t needed unless things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more surgery? I just had one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll watch you closely. If the abscesses shrink with antibiotics, we can avoid another procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea’s better. I haven’t thrown up since the tube was in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to remove the NG tube now and start you on small sips of clear liquids. We’ll see how you tolerate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water or apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with water and clear broth. If you keep that down, we’ll advance to more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well with clear liquids. We’re going to try a soft diet—like toast and applesauce. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. I took the pain meds you gave me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also continuing your home medications, like metformin and lisinopril, since your blood sugar and blood pressure are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my insulin? I usually take Lantus at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a dose last night. We’ll continue it tonight. We’re monitoring your glucose closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two bowel movements today, which is excellent. It means your gut is working. We’ll advance you to a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m actually hungry. Can I have real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll bring you a regular diabetic-friendly meal. We want to make sure you can keep it down before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well overnight—no vomiting, pain controlled, eating and moving around. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. But what about those abscesses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re being treated with antibiotics. Since you’re improving, we’ll switch to oral antibiotics at home. You’ll need to follow up with your surgeon in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I don’t want to run out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, plus stool softeners and laxatives to prevent constipation from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I should call if the pain gets worse or I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also if you develop a fever, see blood in your vomit or stool, or have trouble urinating. Otherwise, keep resting, walking, and taking your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re feeling okay to go home now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready. I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember to avoid heavy lifting and driving on pain meds. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. Take care of yourself.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, PTSD, bipolar disorder, and recent ventral hernia repair presented with worsening mid-abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting after being kicked in the abdomen. He was found to have three rim-enhancing fluid collections near his surgical mesh on CT, concerning for abscesses. He was managed conservatively with NPO status, NG tube decompression, IV fluids, and antibiotics. His symptoms improved, nausea resolved, and he tolerated diet advancement to regular food. He remained afebrile with stable vitals and good pain control. He was discharged home on oral pain medications, stool softeners, and instructions to follow up with his surgeon, with clear guidance on when to seek medical attention.
